The appellant 's father, who was the plaintiff in the suit, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a house in the suit property. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the properties were Khandappa 's self acquisitions and that the properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. The trial Court held that it was a case of a partition and that the property belonged to the family consisting of the joint family and that the joint family was a joint family. The High court held that the property was not a joint family property and that the suit was not maintainable. The High. Court also held that the suit properties did not belong to the joint Hindu family and that, therefore, the properties were not part of the joint Hindu Family properties. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The Hindu Succession Act, 1937, conferred on the Hindu widow the right to a share in the joint family property, and that the right to the share of the widow was not a right to the property. [860 B] The Hindu Succession is a Hindu governed by the Hindu Succession Act. The Hindu Succession provides by section 14(1) that any property possessed by a female Hindu shall be held by her as a full owner thereof and not as a limited owner. By restricting the operation of the fiction created by Explanation I to section 6, the Hindu Succession is not a Hindu governed under the Hindu Succession. The appellant was a crosscutter. He was prosecuted under r. 18 (a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to him. The appellant was served with a charge sheet on him. The enquiry was held and the appellant was reinstated. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal and the High Court held that the order was not a bona fide exercise of power. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the order of the Industrial Tribunal was not a colourable exercise of power and was not a mere administrative order. The order of the Tribunal was not an administrative order and was not an order of the Government. The order was not an executive order and was therefore not a colourable act. The order must be held to be a colourable exercise and must be set aside as a bona fide act. The Tribunal was not competent to decide whether the order was a colourable exercise. The order merely made a report to the Government and the order made under r.18 (a) was a colourable act and was not mala fide. The order made under the r. 18(a) of Standing Orders in this case was not a mala fide exercise of the power conferred. The order in question was not a quasi judicial order and it was not a speaking order. The Tribunal had the right to inquire into the cause and the order had been set aside and action was taken under r. 19(a) and the order of discharge was set aside. The order passed under r.19(a) was not a judicial order and was a colourable order. The appellant had no locus standi to challenge the order. The High Court was right in holding that the order had not been set aside.

The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Board of Directors of the company and the Inspector of Companies. The High Court dismissed the petition. The company appealed to this Court. The company contended that the order of Directors was invalid because it was made by the Chairman of the company. Held, that the order was invalid because the company was not a company within the meaning of section 237(b) of the Companies Act. The order was not invalid because it could not be challenged on the ground that the order had been made by the Board. The order of the High Court was not invalid on the ground of mala fides. The order did not contain any ground for quashing the order of its Board. The High court was right in holding that the order did not make the order invalid because it had been made in contravention of the provisions of section 237 (b) of The Act. The High Courts were not bound to interfere with the order of their Board. The power of the Board to issue a writ of mandamus or other appropriate writ, direction or order quashing the order was not a matter of right. The order passed by the Board was invalid because, it was made in contravention with the provisions of the Act. The Board was not bound to comply with the provisions contained in section 237(a) of the Act and the order was therefore invalid. The order made by the High Court on the ground, that the company was a company within its meaning as defined in section 2(d) of the , and that the order having been made by it, the order of winding up was invalid. The High, Court was right in its view. The order dated May 19, 1965 was not valid because it was passed by the Chairman and the Inspector. The order, therefore, was invalid.

The appellants contended that the conciliation was not pending when the report of the Conciliation Officer was received by the appropriate Government and that the Conciliation Officer had not been given any useful purpose. Held, that the conciliation Proceedings could be said to be pending at the time when the report was received by it. The conciliation proceedings did not come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) of the Act. The termination of the conciliation proceedings was deemed to take place when the report is received by the Government. The conciliation proceeding could be continued only when the report had been received by the State Government. The termination would depend upon how soon a report is received. The conciliation officer is required to bring about settlement between the parties and must begin his investigation without delay and if no settlement is arrived at he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an start. The conciliation is not a mere formality and the termination of the Conciliation proceedings is deemed to take effect as provided in the Act. If the conciliation proceedings are not closed, the proceedings are not terminated. The termination is deemed to have commenced on the expiry of the period of the Conciliation. The termination was deemed to have been terminated by the Conciliation Officer under section 20(1) of the , and the termination was deemed not to take place until the expiry of 14 days but terminate as provided by section 20(3)(b) Of the Act.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of land in the village of the appellants in the village in 1949. The appellants filed an application for review of the order cancelling their allotment of land on the ground that the cancellation of the allotment of the appellants was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land. The Additional Custodian made an order on October 31, 1952 cancelling the allotment of land and allotted the land in favour of the appellants. The appellants preferred an application for the review of the orders cancelling their allotment. The Additional Administrator made an order cancelling the allotment and cancelled the allotment of plots in favour of their father. The appellants appealed to the Custodian General. The appellants contended that the order cancelling the allotments was a result in violation of the provisions of section 19(1) of the Act and that the cancellation was a result on the ground of fraud and that the order was not a nullity. Held, that the order of the Additional Custodian was not a mere order of allotment and that the orders of cancellation were not a nullity and that the impugned order was a nullity. The order of the Deputy Custodian was therefore a nullity. It was not open to the appellants to make out a new case at this stage of the argument. The order was not an order of allotment. The order did not contain any provision for cancellation of allotment and the order of allotment was not a valid order. The order merely stated that the order had been made in contravention of the provisions contained in section 19(2) of the. Act. The order had no application to the facts of the case. The order dated October 31,1952 was a nullity and the order was a void one. The order could not be said to be a nullity.
